stops.name: Troyes, the Council and the Rule of the Templars
stops.campa: At the Council of Troyes the poor knights of Hugh de Payns, guardians of the pilgrim roads to Jerusalem, are given a Rule and made a religious order of the Church. Bernard's hand is on the drafting; his authority reconciles the sword with the cloister, the monk with the warrior. Here is born the Order of the Temple: the white mantle, the red cross, the vow. From this small synod in Champagne descends the vast Templar power, and the men who will one day burn for it. What Bernard writes at Troyes, Jacques de Molay will die defending on the Île aux Juifs.

stops.name: Clairvaux, In Praise of the New Knighthood
stops.campa: For Hugh de Payns, whose knights waver, doubting whether monks may shed blood, Bernard writes the Liber ad milites Templi de laude novae militiae: In Praise of the New Knighthood. He proclaims a new kind of soldier who fights a double war, against flesh and blood and against spiritual evil; who kills not homicide but malicide, slaying not the man but the sin; who cannot lose, for to die in Christ or to slay for Christ is alike gain. He praises them fearless and unwashed, their swords for the wicked, and glorifies the holy places their arms defend.
stops.quote: The knight of Christ, I say, kills with a good conscience and dies with a better. When he dies, he benefits himself; when he kills, he benefits Christ. He does not bear the sword in vain; he is God's minister for the punishment of evildoers.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, Liber ad milites Templi de laude novae militiae, III

stops.name: Étampes, the synod that chooses Innocent II
stops.campa: The papacy is torn: two men elected, Innocent II fleeing to France and Anacletus II holding Rome by the Frangipani. King Louis the Fat gathers the bishops of France at Étampes and asks them to judge. They put the whole question into the hands of one man: the abbot of Clairvaux. Bernard, after prayer, declares for Innocent, and his word becomes the verdict of the French Church. From this hour the frail monk is the arbiter of Christendom, carrying the true pope through the courts of kings and the cities of the schism.

stops.name: Parthenay (La Coudre), the Duke of Aquitaine falls before the Host
stops.campa: William X, Duke of Aquitaine, great and violent, clings to the antipope and has driven out bishops loyal to Innocent. Bernard, unable to move him by words, celebrates Mass while the excommunicate duke waits outside the church door. At the consecration Bernard takes up the Body of the Lord upon the paten and comes out to the threshold, his face terrible, and holds the Host toward the armed man, commanding him to submit to God whose servants he despises. William, huge and mail-clad, goes rigid, foams, and falls to the earth as one dead. He rises broken, obeys, and is reconciled; the schism loses its strongest sword.
stops.quote: Here is the Son of the Virgin, the Head and Lord of the Church you persecute. Here is your Judge, at whose name every knee shall bow. Will you despise him as you despise his servants?
stops.quote_source: Vita Prima Bernardi, on the reconciliation of William X

stops.name: Milan, the city won for the pope
stops.campa: Bernard crosses the Alps into Italy for Innocent, reconciling Pisa with Genoa and, hardest of all, the great commune of Milan with the pope. The Milanese pour out to meet him, mob him for the hem of his habit, snatch threads to keep as relics, carry him through the streets. They would make him their archbishop; he flees the honor. In the schism's cities he is peacemaker, envoy, wonder-worker, the little abbot of the Bright Valley moving Italy as a shepherd moves his flock, until Anacletus dies and Rome falls at last to the pope Bernard made.

stops.name: Rome: the antipope dead, the schism ended
stops.campa: Bernard comes to Rome itself in the pope's train. Anacletus dies in January 1138 and a rump elects Victor IV in his place, but Bernard, by pleading and the sheer weight of his holiness, persuades Victor to lay down the tiara and submit. The eight-year schism that split kingdoms and armies closes without a war; Innocent II reigns alone. The little abbot of the Bright Valley has healed the deepest wound in Christendom by the labor of his tongue and his feet, city after city, king after king; and then, wanting nothing Rome could give, he turns home to his monks.

stops.name: Sens, the hammer of Abelard
stops.campa: At the Council of Sens, before archbishops and King Louis VII, Bernard meets Peter Abelard, the sharpest dialectician of the age, whose reason he holds is dissolving the mysteries of the faith. Bernard has already gathered the suspect propositions, letter by letter, and arraigns them one after another. Abelard, seeing not a debate but a tribunal, rises and appeals to Rome rather than answer, and departs. The council condemns his teachings; Bernard's letters to the Curia seal the sentence. The subtle master is silenced, and Bernard stands as the guardian of orthodoxy, the watchdog of Aleth's dream.
stops.quote: Peter Abelard is trying to make void the merit of Christian faith, when he deems himself able by human reason to comprehend God altogether. He ascends to the heavens and descends even to the abyss; nothing may hide from him.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, Epistola 190 (to Pope Innocent II), against Abelard

stops.name: Toulouse and Albi, against the heretics of the Midi
stops.campa: The south of France is stirred by the preaching of Henry of Lausanne, who empties the churches and turns the people against the priesthood; a foretaste of the Cathar tide. Bernard, old and worn, is called down to Languedoc. He preaches at Albi, Toulouse, Verfeil, and the crowds come back to the Church; wonders and healings mark his passage, and the story is told of a possessed woman whose torment he breaks. The Vita Prima closes its record of his life with this journey: the watchdog barking, as Aleth dreamed, against the enemies of the faith to the very end.
stops.quote: The faith is to be produced by persuasion, not imposed by force. Heretics are to be caught rather than driven off — caught, I say, not by arms but by arguments.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, Sermon 64 on the Song of Songs, on the heretics

stops.name: Vézelay, the preaching of the Second Crusade
stops.campa: On the hill of the Magdalene at Vézelay, at Easter, before King Louis VII and Queen Eleanor and a multitude too great for the church, Bernard mounts a wooden platform on the slope and preaches the cross. Edessa has fallen; the pope's bull names Bernard the preacher of the war. He cries out God's offer of pardon to all who take the cross, and the crowd roars 'Crosses! Crosses!' The prepared cloth crosses run out; Bernard tears his own habit into strips to make more. Kings, lords, and thousands are signed with the cross by his hand in a single day.
stops.quote: Take the sign of the cross. At once you shall have indulgence for all the sins which you confess with a contrite heart. The cloth itself sells for little; if it be worn on a faithful shoulder it is worth the kingdom of God.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, crusade preaching and letters (Epistola 363, to the English people)

stops.name: Mainz, the mob against the Jews turned back
stops.campa: In the Rhineland a renegade monk, Radulf, preaches that the Jews are the enemies within and stirs the mobs to slaughter: at Cologne, Mainz, Worms, Speyer, the old massacres threatening again. Bernard leaves France and comes down the Rhine to stop it. He confronts Radulf at Mainz, silences him, and sends him back to his cloister for breaking obedience and preaching without leave. He forbids the killing in sermon and in letter, teaching that the Jews are living witnesses and must not be touched: whoever lays hands on a Jew lays hands on Jesus himself.
stops.quote: It is an act of Christian piety both to vanquish the proud and to spare the subjected, especially those for whom we have a law and a promise. The Jews are not to be persecuted, killed, or even put to flight.
stops.quote_source: Bernard, Epistola 363, on the Jews and the Crusade

stops.name: Frankfurt, the king wavers before the abbot
stops.campa: At the imperial diet in Frankfurt Bernard meets King Conrad III, who holds back from the crusade, judging it folly to leave the Empire for the East. Bernard presses him, but the king will not yield here; the abbot bides, following the court on toward Speyer for the Christmas feast, where he means to lay the whole weight of the Last Judgment on Conrad's conscience. Even now, unbending kings bend to him in the end, the frail monk who commands armies without a sword, moving the crowned heads of Christendom as a shepherd moves a stubborn flock.

stops.name: Constance and Freiburg, the preaching in the tongue he does not speak
stops.campa: Bernard passes up the Rhine through the German lands preaching the cross, though he speaks no German. He preaches in Latin or French; an interpreter renders him after; yet the chroniclers marvel that the crowds are moved more by his untranslated words than by the interpreter's, weeping and taking the cross before they understand a syllable, so that the moving of hearts is laid to God and not to speech. At Constance, Freiburg, Basel and along the road, miracles multiply at his every step: the blind, the lame, the mute healed as he passes.
